audit_scope.description: This batch covers EL components including: EVM execution (SELFDESTRUCT, control flow opcodes, environment opcodes), transaction submission interfaces (JSON-RPC), blob transaction processing (EIP-4844), and network upgrade coordination. The external entities interact with the EL through transaction submission, contract deployment, and blob data submission.

in_scope: Control flow opcodes (JUMP, JUMPI, STOP, PC, GAS)
Environment opcodes (BALANCE, EXTCODESIZE, EXTCODEHASH, CALLDATALOAD, CALLDATACOPY, RETURNDATALOAD, RETURNDATACOPY, BLOBHASH, BLOBBASEFEE)
Network upgrade activation at block numbers
Gas metering and cold/warm account access tracking
out_of_scope: Contract source code or smart contract logic (trust model focuses on EL infrastructure)

trusted_external_entities.name: User via Transaction (JSON-RPC or P2P)
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: JSON-RPC endpoints (eth_sendTransaction, eth_sendRawTransaction) or P2P transaction gossip
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External users submit transactions that trigger contract execution, including SELFDESTRUCT operations. This is unauthenticated public input that must be fully validated. Transactions contain arbitrary calldata, value transfers, and can invoke any contract function. The transaction data field is entirely attacker-controlled.
threat_scenarios: Malicious calldata could trigger unexpected contract behavior
SELFDESTRUCT could be used in reentrancy attacks or to destroy critical contracts
Transaction with crafted data could exploit EVM validation bugs

trusted_external_entities.name: Contract Deployer via Transaction
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Contract creation transactions (to=null) via JSON-RPC or P2P
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External entity that deploys smart contracts with arbitrary bytecode. The deployer controls JUMPDEST placement and all contract logic. While the EVM validates jump destinations, the deployer is untrusted and could attempt to create malicious bytecode patterns. The deployed code persists in state and executes when invoked.
threat_scenarios: Deployer could create contract with malicious jump patterns to exploit validation bugs
Contract bytecode could contain hidden backdoors or vulnerabilities
Constructor could perform malicious state changes during deployment

trusted_external_entities.name: Decentralized Application (DApp) via JSON-RPC
trusted_external_entities.rationale: DApps interact with EL through JSON-RPC, submitting transactions with ABI metadata. The DApp is untrusted - it can provide arbitrary, potentially misleading ABI information to deceive users. Even though function signature is validated, the ABI display name and parameter descriptions are fully controlled by the DApp and could be deceptive. This is a phishing/social engineering vector.
data_flows: Function signature -> Validation against transaction data
threat_scenarios: Malicious DApp provides misleading ABI to deceive users (e.g., displaying 'transfer' but actually calling 'approve')
Function selector collision - different function with same 4-byte hash
ABI parameter names crafted to look legitimate but execute malicious logic
DApp exploits wallet's ABI parsing vulnerabilities with malformed JSON

trusted_external_entities.name: Wallet User (Human)
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Wallet software approval UI (indirectly affects transaction submission)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: End users make trust decisions based on wallet-displayed information. However, users are untrusted from the EL's perspective - they can be deceived by social engineering, approve malicious transactions, or have compromised devices. User approval is not a security boundary for the EL itself; the EL must validate all transaction data regardless of user intent. Users operate outside the system boundary and send data IN via wallet software.
threat_scenarios: User deceived into approving malicious transaction despite warnings
Compromised user device signs transactions without user knowledge
User falls victim to phishing displaying fake transaction details

trusted_external_entities.name: Blob Transaction Submitter via JSON-RPC
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: JSON-RPC transaction submission for type-3 blob transactions
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External entity submitting EIP-4844 blob transactions with versioned hashes. The submitter controls blob versioned hashes and blob data. While blobs are primarily for data availability (CL scope), the EL processes blob transactions and makes versioned hashes available to contracts via BLOBHASH opcode. Blob submitter is untrusted and could provide malicious blob references or attempt to exploit blob transaction validation.
data_flows: Blob versioned hashes -> blob_versioned_hashes list in EVM
Blob transaction data -> EVM execution context
threat_scenarios: Submitter provides invalid blob versioned hashes to cause transaction failures
Contract logic depends on blob hash values controlled by untrusted submitter
Blob index manipulation to access unintended blob data

trusted_external_entities.name: Ethereum Core Developers (Network Upgrade Coordination)
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Governance process for setting network upgrade activation block numbers
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Core developers coordinate network upgrades by selecting activation block numbers. This is SEMI_TRUSTED because while there is a governance process and community oversight, the selection of specific block numbers is a trusted administrative action that could cause disruption if done maliciously or incorrectly. However, the actual enforcement happens through client software updates which node operators must voluntarily install, providing some distributed trust. This is an authenticated governance channel but the output (upgrade schedule) affects all nodes.
data_flows: Block number estimation -> Client software hardcoded activation blocks
threat_scenarios: Malicious core dev proposes upgrade with insufficient lead time causing network disruption
Incorrect block number estimation causes upgrade to activate at unexpected time
Rushed critical upgrade introduces vulnerabilities due to insufficient testing

trusted_external_entities.name: Client Development Teams
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Client software implementation of network upgrades
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Client teams implement network upgrades in execution client software (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon, etc.). This is SEMI_TRUSTED because while these teams are known and accountable, implementation bugs or backdoors are possible. Node operators trust client teams by running their software. Client teams operate in a semi-authenticated environment with code review and community oversight, but they have significant control over the actual implementation of protocol rules.
data_flows: Client software updates -> Node operator deployments
threat_scenarios: Client implementation bug causes consensus split at upgrade activation
Malicious client team introduces backdoor in upgrade implementation
Client teams disagree on specification interpretation causing divergent implementations

trusted_external_entities.name: Node Operators
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Node software installation and configuration decisions
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Node operators run EL client software and must update before network upgrades. From the network's perspective, node operators are UNTRUSTED - they may fail to upgrade, run modified clients, or deliberately stay on old versions. While operators are essential to the network, they operate outside the protocol's control boundary. The network must tolerate malicious or non-upgrading operators without breaking consensus.
threat_scenarios: Operators fail to upgrade causing chain split risk
Operators run modified clients with non-standard behavior
Coordinated operator attack running malicious client versions

trusted_external_entities.name: Transaction Sender (Calldata Provider)
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Transaction input data field in submitted transactions
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External entity providing calldata in transactions. This is the same as EXT-TRANSACTION but explicitly focused on the calldata aspect. Transaction senders control all input data including function selectors, parameters, and arbitrary data bytes. The EVM must validate calldata access bounds and handle malformed or malicious calldata safely. This is completely untrusted public input.
threat_scenarios: Malformed calldata exploits parsing vulnerabilities
Out-of-bounds calldata access attempts
Calldata crafted to exploit contract logic vulnerabilities
Excessive calldata size for DoS attacks

boundary_edges.description: External transaction crosses trust boundary into EVM execution engine. Transaction data (calldata, value) flows from untrusted external source into contract execution context.
validation_required: Gas limit and gas price validation

boundary_edges.description: DApp submits transaction via JSON-RPC eth_sendTransactionToContractFunction with ABI metadata. ABI data crosses trust boundary from untrusted DApp to wallet/provider for display.
validation_required: Function signature hash matching against transaction data

boundary_edges.description: DApp provides ABI metadata for transaction display. This is explicitly marked as untrusted input that could be deceptive.
validation_required: ABI function selector must match transaction data prefix
Warning displayed to user about untrusted ABI source

boundary_edges.description: Transaction sender's calldata is accessed by contract via CALLDATALOAD. Calldata from external untrusted source flows into EVM memory/stack operations.
validation_required: Offset bounds checking (handled by buffer_read with zero-padding)

boundary_edges.description: Blob transaction submitter's versioned hashes are accessed via BLOBHASH opcode. Blob references from external untrusted source flow into contract execution.
validation_required: Blob index bounds checking (returns zero for out-of-bounds)

boundary_edges.description: Contract deployer's bytecode crosses trust boundary into state storage and execution environment. Deployed code is scanned for JUMPDEST markers.
validation_required: JUMPDEST scanning to build valid_jump_destinations whitelist
Init code execution with gas metering

boundary_edges.description: Core developers propose network upgrades through governance process. This is a semi-trusted administrative action that affects network-wide behavior.
validation_required: Lead time requirements (2-6 weeks depending on upgrade type)

boundary_edges.description: Client teams implement upgrades in software that node operators run. This is semi-trusted implementation of protocol specifications.
validation_required: Code review by other client teams and community

boundary_edges.description: Node operators deploy client software updates. While operators are untrusted individually, the network relies on sufficient honest operators upgrading.
validation_required: No direct validation possible - social coordination
Network monitoring for upgrade adoption rates

coverage_analysis.notes: All 9 unique external entities identified across the 5 files have associated boundary edges. Coverage is complete. EXT-USER (wallet user) implicitly crosses boundary through EXT-DAPP and EXT-TRANSACTION entities - users operate wallets that submit transactions, so they are covered by transaction submission boundaries.
